properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: This project is located between Wautoma and Montello just one and a half miles west of the old DNR Discovery Center (intersection of Hwy 22 and Dixie Ave). Large adult brown trout that overwinter in the lower Mecan River seek thermal refuge in the Chaffee Creek during the summer months and migrate through this area to spawn in the fall. Public hunting and fishing lands are abundant in this area. A DNR parking area is located at the downstream end of the project section located off of 14th Ave. Trout population monitoring surveys have seen a decline in the numbers of adult fish over the past decade through this section. Overhead cover and pool habitats have been lost due to excessive amounts of sand eroding from unstable streambanks, where Reed Canary Grass dominates. The goals of the project are as follows: -Increase adult trout habitats with the installation of submerged tree structures, conventional overhead bank covers, and plunge pools/riffles. -Stabilize actively eroding streambanks to reduce sand infiltration with the installation of conventional overhead bank covers and by deflecting main channel flow with coarse wood structures. -Enhance fishability by mechanically removing over growth exotic woody vegetation from the stream banks.  Oak wilt has been a severe issue through out this area as well making the stream inaccessible to hunters and anglers as well.

properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Peterson Creek is located between Waupaca, to the south, and Scandinavia, to the north. properties.SITENAMECOMBINED: Radley Creek - Dayton Rd
properties.PROJECTPURPOSE:
This section of the Radley Creek flows parallel to Hwy 22 between Waupaca, to the north, and Wautoma, to the south, and through a large parcel of the Radley Creek State Fishery Area containing three large DNR parking areas. Damaging storms over the past decade have knocked excessive numbers of large trees into the stream corridor. These fallen trees have made angling next to impossible, have caused the deterioration of main channel definition, and have eroded fine sediments from the streambanks. The influx of sediment into the river has filled in natural pools and has reduced the quality and quantity of overhead and refuge cover.
The goals of the project are as follows: 
-Enhance fishability by reorienting storm damaged trees and by removing over grown, exotic woody vegetation from the streambanks.
-Improve the natural ability of the river to transport fine sediments, deposit these sediments outside of the main channel, and to scour pools. This will be accomplished by reorienting fallen trees and by using the cut woody vegetation for the installation of brush bundles.
-Enhance juvenile trout habitats, specifically refuge cover, by using the cut limbs and woody vegetation for the installation of brush bundles along the main channel.
-Enhance adult trout habitats, specifically overhead and cover habitats, by optimizing the natural recruitment of coarse wood through the reorientation of storm damaged trees.
properties.TECHNIQUESSTRUCTURES: Brush bundle/matresses, Brush Removal, Log/brush/rock shelters

properties.SITENAMECOMBINED: Rowan Creek - State Highway 51
properties.PROJECTPURPOSE:
The purpose of this project was to:

1.) Remove woody vegetation from approximately 1,250 feet of the Rowan Creek corridor, leaving hardwoods and selected evergreens standing wherever possible.  This was done to increase sunlight penetration to the stream (increase primary productivity and invertebrate community) and banks (re-establish grassy vegetation), as well as to improve fishability for anglers.  Leaving strategic hardwoods in place will ensure a seed bank for future re-generation of desirable hardwoods, primarily for oak species, secondarily for black walnut.

2.) Establish grassy vegetation on the stream banks to stabilize bank sediments, thereby decreasing sediment inputs to the stream during runoff events.

3.) Stabilize the toe of the bank with large rock to prevent erosion of the bank by the stream.

4.) Increase the amount of overhead cover for trout in order to increase the number of larger trout inhabiting this segment of Rowan Creek.  This was to be accomplished two ways: increase depth of existing pools by using current management devices to direct flow and increase scour and thus pool depth, and by adding rock or wood structure to the stream as hiding cover.

properties.SITENAMECOMBINED: West Branch White River - Hwy Y
properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Initial land acquisition efforts by the DNR on the White River and its cold water tributaries began back in 1948 with the purchase of a 200 acre farm along the banks of the Main Branch of the White River. Today, the DNR now manages over 2,000 acres of land throughout the system. Some of the earliest instream trout habitat improvement structures in Wisconsin can be found throughout this system, dating back to the days of the WPA and CCC work camps of the 1930's. Remnant structures can still be found on the West Branch of the White River and are believed to be a contributing factor to why this river supports one of the few naturally reproducing populations of rainbow trout in the state. The project site is located on a newly purchased (2012) DNR property just downstream of some of these structures on Highway Y, a mile south of Highway 21 west of Wautoma.  An excessive amount of storm damaged trees lay in the stream corridor through this wild section of river. These fallen trees are dissipating the flow of the main channel which is resulting in streambank erosion. Tree growth in this segment of Rowan Creek has led to a loss of grassy cover in the stream corridor. properties.PROJECTPURPOSE:
The South Fork of the White River is cold headwater tributary to the White River and premier trout stream to both Bayfield County and the State of Wisconsin.  The South Fork supports viable sport fisheries for both brown and brook trout and is also known to support spawning migrations of brown trout from the White River’s mainstem.  The entire stream thread lies within the White River Fishery Area, which was established in 1961 to insure public access to this unique resource and to protect this sensitive watershed from logging and development pressures.  Prior to acquisition by the state, much of the South Fork’s 2.3 miles of stream thread was impounded by a series of artificial lakes maintained by previous proprietors for trout propagation and private fishing.  Through WDNR efforts ranging from dam removal, dredging, and intensive channel work much of the stream has been restored.
     Although past restorations efforts included stream brushing much of the streams riparian corridor is densely vegetated and dominated by the exotic shrubs common buckthorn (Rhamus cathartica) and glossy buckthorn (Rhamnus frangula).  The invasive shrubs dominate the riparian forest community resulting in allelopathic elimination of native forest species.  Buckthorn dominance in the riparian flora is reducing vegetative diversity and is inhibiting regeneration of large woody species native to lowland forests and beneficial to stream ecosystems.  The dense buckthorn canopy is also resulting in an overly shaded stream environment, thereby reducing stream productivity.  In addition, densely shaded stream threads lack aquatic vegetation which provides important cover for juvenile trout and non-game fish species.

properties.SITENAMECOMBINED: South Fork of the White River Habitat Development
properties.PROJECTPURPOSE:
The South Fork of the White River is a headwater tributary to the White River and premier trout stream to both Bayfield County and the State of Wisconsin.  The South Fork supports viable sport fisheries for both brown and brook trout and is also known to support spawning migrations of brown trout from the White River’s mainstem.  The entire stream thread lies within the White River Fishery Area, which was established in 1961 to insure public access to this unique resource and to protect this sensitive watershed from logging and development pressures.  Prior to acquisition by the state, much of the South Fork’s 2.3 miles of stream thread was impounded by a series of artificial lakes maintained by previous proprietors for trout propagation and private fishing.  Through WDNR efforts ranging from dam removal, dredging, and intensive channel work much of the stream has been restored.

Although past restorations efforts included stream-bank brushing much of the streams riparian corridor is now densely vegetated, largely by the exotic shrubs common buckthorn (Rhamus cathartica) and glossy buckthorn (Rhamnus frangula).  These invasive shrubs dominate the riparian forest community resulting in allelopathic elimination of native forest species.  This dominance has resulted in reduced vegetative diversity along the riparian corridor and poor regeneration of large woody species beneficial to stream ecosystems.  In addition, dense buckthorn canopies are resulting in overly shaded stream environments, inhibiting macrophyte growth important to stabilizing stream sediments and providing cover for juvenile salmonids.
Riparian control of invasive buckthorns will help improve biotic and abiotic conditions for trout and aid the recruitment of large woody species critical to the stream’s future health.  No effort to control these species only stands to upset the important relationship between riparian habitat and stream quality and seems contrary to the Department priority of invasive species control.

properties.SITENAMECOMBINED: White River - Cottonville Ave
properties.PROJECTPURPOSE:
The town of Wautoma was established in the late 1800's on the banks of the White River and its tributaries. Project location is just two miles south of town and provides anglers with one of the best opportunities in Wisconsin to catch larger than average brown trout and occasionally a beautiful rainbow trout. The stories and history of trout angling through out this river are countless. One example of the love for this stream and it's angling lore is the book "Le Shack: A Very Special Fishing Place" by Jim Chapralis.  The angler stories center around a cabin located just upstream of the current project location.  There is a bench commemorating Le Shack and Mr. Chapralis located at a public parking area just east of the Cottonville Rd bridge.
This section of river is a popular angling destination in Central Wisconsin. Especially during the famous nighttime "Hex Hatch" which occurs during the months of June through July when adult Hexagenia limbata mayflies emerge. 
While this sand dominated, lower reach of river has many issues working against the trout populations and angling opportunity, the issue that effects trout habitats most directly is the dominance of the invasive, exotic Reed Canary Grass (RCG) throughout the White River floodplain. The rhizomal root systems of RCG grow laterally along impenetrable native streambank substrates, such as peat. This growth results in streambank fragmentation of large, mobile RCG vegetative mats, which also contain the uppermost layers of native riparian substrate. Each vegetative mat lost from the streambank results in a domino effect of fragmentation and stream widening. The rivers natural ability to transport sediment and deposit them outside of the main channel is compromised and trout habitats, such as deep pools, are filled in with sand.
The goals of the project are as follows: 
-Stabilize streambanks by protecting actively eroding streambanks with christmas trees and dredged sand spoils. 
-Improve the natural ability of the river to transport fine sediments, deposit these sediments outside of the main channel, and to scour pools. This will be accomplished by installing wing deflectors composed of christmas trees, cut brush, coarse wood, and sand spoils.
-Enhance adult trout habitats, specifically overhead and cover habitats, by installing submerged tree structures.
-Excessive amounts of sand have created a broad, shallow flat just above the White River Flowage.  Adult trout are known to over winter in the flowage proper. Habitat improvements hope to reconnect the upper river for trout migration out of the flowage by scouring a channel through this shallow zone.
-Work completed through this project will increase angler opportunities by providing more deep water holding cover areas adjacent to refuge cover as well.
properties.TECHNIQUESSTRUCTURES: Brush bundle/matresses, Brush Removal, Channel shaping, Log/brush/rock shelters, Wing Deflector

properties.SITENAMECOMBINED: Rowan Creek - Loveland Rd.
properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Rowan Creek is a popular destination for trout anglers in Columbia County, the greater Madison area, and beyond.  Rowan Creek Fishery Area provides the best combination of good public trout fishing and stream accessibility/fishability in Columbia County.  The portion of Rowan Creek where the work will take place is Class I brown trout water.  Habitat improvement work was completed on a segment of stream immediately downstream from the prospective project in the late 1970s.  The improvements made at that time have held up well over the years and are still benefiting the fishery today.  This project will extend the area of improved trout habitat and link it to an easy public access point.  Tree growth in this segment of Rowan Creek has led to a loss of grassy cover in the stream corridor.  This has contributed to bank erosion and widening of the stream, as well an increase in the amount of sediment entering the stream.  Growth of trees along the stream corridor also reduces productivity in the stream by reducing the amount of sunlight reaching the water.  Trout populations eventually decline as a result of the loss of overhead cover as the stream widens and loses depth, as well as from the reduced productivity from decreased light penetration.  Stream productivity and stability of the stream bank would be enhanced by tree and brush removal and re-establishment of grassy cover on the banks.  Grassy vegetation will do a better job of holding the soil together as well as filtering runoff and reducing sediment loading into the stream.  Tree removal will also increase light penetration to the stream which will increase primary productivity.  Armoring the toe of the streambank with rock riprap will help ensure that future bank erosion does not occur.  This ensures the stream will not lose depth through erosion and progressive widening, and it will also reduce sediment loading into the stream.  Installation of current management devices and LUNKER structures will improve the amount of overhead cover for trout by increasing areas of scour and providing artificial hiding places (LUNKERS) for trout.

Future phases will focus on other areas of SBOR and separate permits will be obtained for any future work outside of the current project area.  Many of the trees are willows that have fallen or are leaning perpendicular to the stream and have impeded navigation and resulted in wider, shallower areas.  As a result, we've received complaints from some landowners and anglers which prompted us to seek and receive WDNR Trout Stamp funds for a habitat improvement project to improve fish habitat, fishing opportunities, and navigability of the stream.  WDNR staff from the Wild Rose Operations crew will use chainsaws and gas-powered winches (no heavy equipment) to cut and reposition trees at angles to make the woody debris more beneficial as trout habitat in the stream.  Any trees requiring anchoring will be anchored with galvanized steel cable, duckbill anchors, and cable clamps.  Much of the work will be done on state lands in the SBOR Fishery Area; but there may be some trees on private lands within the riparian zone adjacent to the stream that may need cutting or repositioning.  This project will improve navigation and fish habitat on approximately 3 miles of stream.

properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Eagle Creek is a Class III trout water. Evaluation of the WI Priority Watershed Program for Improving Stream Habitat and Fish Communities (1994) documented a much improved aquatic system with substantially reduced bank erosion and improved bank vegetation. However, there was no notice of a rebound in the trout fisher. Later surveys conducted in 2001 and 2007 found natural reproduction of brook trout in the upstream segment and adults ranging from 4-14 inches downstream. properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: The South Fork of the White River is a headwater tributary to the White River and premier trout stream to both Bayfield County and the State of Wisconsin.  The South Fork supports viable sport fisheries for both brown and brook trout and is also known to support spawning migrations of brown trout from the White River’s mainstem.  The entire stream thread lies within the White River Fishery Area, which was established in 1961 to insure public access to this unique resource and to protect this sensitive watershed from logging and development pressures.  Prior to acquisition by the state, much of the South Fork’s 2.3 miles of stream thread was impounded by a series of artificial lakes maintained by previous proprietors for trout propagation and private fishing.  Through WDNR efforts ranging from dam removal, dredging, and intensive channel work much of the stream has been restored.Although past restorations efforts included stream-bank brushing much of the streams riparian corridor is now densely vegetated by the exotic shrub, glossy buckthorn, (Rhamnus frangula).  This invasive shrub dominates the riparian forest community resulting in allelopathic elimination of native forest species. The dominance of this shrub has resulted in reduced vegetative diversity along the riparian corridor and poor regeneration of large woody species beneficial to stream ecosystems.  In addition, dense buckthorn canopies are resulting in overly shaded stream environments, inhibiting macrophyte growth important to stabilizing stream sediments and providing cover for juvenile salmonids.  Riparian control of invasive buckthorns will help improve biotic and abiotic conditions for trout and aid the recruitment of large woody species critical to the stream’s future health. Dense riparian growth of glossy buckthorn also hinders angler access to this popular fishing stream and limits opportunities for future in-stream projects in currently unimproved stream reaches.   No effort to control this detrimental species only stands to upset the important relationship between riparian and stream health and seems contrary to the Department priority of invasive species control.

Initial land acquisition efforts by the DNR on the White River and its cold water tributaries began back in 1948 with the purchase of a 200 acre farm along the banks of the Main Branch of the White River. Some of the earliest instream trout habitat improvement structures in Wisconsin can be found throughout this system, dating back to the days of the WPA and CCC work camps of the 1930's. properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Habitat improvement work was completed on a segment of stream immediately downstream from the prospective project in the late 1970s.  The improvements made at that time have held up well over the years and are still benefiting the fishery today.  This project will extend the area of improved trout habitat and link it to an easy public access point.  Tree growth in this segment of Rowan Creek has led to a loss of grassy cover in the stream corridor.  This has contributed to bank erosion and widening of the stream, as well an increase in the amount of sediment entering the stream.  Growth of trees along the stream corridor also reduces productivity in the stream by reducing the amount of sunlight reaching the water.  Trout populations eventually decline as a result of the loss of overhead cover as the stream widens and loses depth, as well as from the reduced productivity from decreased light penetration.  Stream productivity and stability of the stream bank would be enhanced by tree and brush removal and re-establishment of grassy cover on the banks.  Grassy vegetation will do a better job of holding the soil together as well as filtering runoff and reducing sediment loading into the stream.  Tree removal will also increase light penetration to the stream which will increase primary productivity.  Armoring the toe of the streambank with rock riprap will help ensure that future bank erosion does not occur.  This ensures the stream will not lose depth through erosion and progressive widening, and it will also reduce sediment loading into the stream.  Installation of current management devices and LUNKER structures will improve the amount of overhead cover for trout by increasing areas of scour and providing artificial hiding places (LUNKERS) for trout.

properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Although past restorations efforts included stream-bank brushing much of the streams riparian corridor is now densely vegetated by the exotic shrub, glossy buckthorn, (Rhamnus frangula).  This invasive shrub dominates the riparian forest community resulting in allelopathic elimination of native forest species. The dominance of this shrub has resulted in reduced vegetative diversity along the riparian corridor and poor regeneration of large woody species beneficial to stream ecosystems.  In addition, dense buckthorn canopies are resulting in overly shaded stream environments, inhibiting macrophyte growth important to stabilizing stream sediments and providing cover for juvenile salmonids.  Riparian control of invasive buckthorns will help improve biotic and abiotic conditions for trout and aid the recruitment of large woody species critical to the stream’s future health.  Dense riparian growth of glossy buckthorn also hinders angler access to this popular fishing stream and limits access for future in-stream projects in currently unimproved stream reaches.   No effort to control this detrimental species only stands to upset the important relationship between riparian and stream health and seems contrary to the Department priority of invasive species control.

properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Initial land acquisition efforts by the DNR on the White River and its cold water tributaries began back in 1948 with the purchase of a 200 acre farm along the banks of the Main Branch of the White River. Today, the DNR now manages over 2,000 acres of land throughout the system. Some of the earliest instream trout habitat improvement structures in Wisconsin can be found throughout this system, dating back to the days of the WPA and CCC work camps of the 1930's. Remnant structures can still be found on the West Branch of the White River and are believed to be a contributing factor to why this river supports one of the few naturally reproducing populations of rainbow trout in the state. The project site is located on a newly purchased (2012) DNR property just downstream of some of these structures on Highway Y, a mile south of Highway 21 west of Wautoma.  An excessive amount of storm damaged trees lay in the stream corridor through this wild section of river. These fallen trees are dissipating the flow of the main channel which is resulting in streambank erosion. Trout habitat, such as overhead cover and deep pools, are filling in with eroding sediments and the stream is becoming wider and shallower. Wading and angling is impossible through the worst of the storm damaged areas. While this wild parcel of property has been relatively unaltered by land use practices, it is riddled with exotic vegetation such as Common Buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) and European Barberry (Berberis vulgaris). The goals of the project are as follows:  -Reorient storm damaged trees to improve wading and angling, and to optimize the natural recruitment of coarse wood into the stream for overhead, refuge, and holding trout habitats. -Stabilize eroding streambanks by installing conventional overhead bank covers and wing deflector structures. -Increase amount of trout spawning substrate through installation of current deflecting structures. -Remove exotic vegetation to promote a diverse community of native vegetation.
properties.TECHNIQUESSTRUCTURES: overhead bank cover, brush bundle/mattresses, log sills, exotic vegetation removal, brush removal, angler/hunter paths

properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: To restore stream connectivity, the Wisconsin Department of Transportation (WisDOT) partnered with the WDNR to obtain a Great Lakes Restoration Initiative grant from the Federal Highway Administration to replace the STH 21 culvert on the West Branch of the White River. A portion of this grant was gifted to the Wild Rose Operations Crew to restore trout habitats within 500 feet above and 500 feet below the new culvert. properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: The town of Wautoma was established in the late 1800's on the banks of the White River and its tributaries. Project location is just two miles south of town and provides anglers with one of the best opportunities in Wisconsin to catch larger than average brown trout and occasionally a beautiful rainbow trout. The stories and history of trout angling through out this river are countless. One example of the love for this stream and it's angling lore is the book "Le Shack: A Very Special Fishing Place" by Jim Chapralis.  The angler stories center around a cabin located just upstream of the current project location.  There is a bench commemorating Le Shack and Mr. Chapralis located at a public parking area just east of the Cottonville Ln bridge. This section of river is a popular angling destination in Central Wisconsin. Especially during the famous nighttime "Hex Hatch" which occurs during the months of June through July when adult Hexagenia limbata mayflies emerge.  While this sand dominated, lower reach of river has many issues working against the trout populations and angling opportunity, the issue that effects trout habitat most directly is the dominance of the invasive, exotic Reed Canary Grass (RCG) throughout the White River floodplain. The rhizomal root systems of RCG grow laterally along impenetrable native streambank substrates, such as peat. This growth results in streambank fragmentation of large, mobile RCG vegetative mats, which also contain the uppermost layers of native riparian substrate. Each vegetative mat lost from the streambank results in a domino effect of fragmentation and stream widening. The rivers natural ability to transport sediment and deposit them outside of the main channel is compromised and trout habitat, such as deep pools, are filled in with sand. The goals of the project are as follows: -Stabilize streambanks by protecting actively eroding streambanks with christmas trees and dredged sand spoils.  -Improve the natural ability of the river to transport fine sediments, deposit these sediments outside of the main channel, and to scour pools. This will be accomplished by installing wing deflectors composed of christmas trees, cut brush, coarse wood, and sand spoils. -Enhance adult trout habitats, specifically overhead and cover habitats, by installing submerged tree structures. -Excessive amounts of sand have created a broad, shallow flat just above the White River Flowage.  Adult trout are known to over winter in the flowage proper. Habitat improvements hope to reconnect the upper river for trout migration out of the flowage by scouring a channel through this shallow zone. -Work completed through this project will increase angler opportunities by providing more deep water holding cover areas adjacent to refuge cover as well.
properties.TECHNIQUESSTRUCTURES: channel shaping, stream re-establishment, native tree/shrub planting, log sills, exotic vegetation removal, brush bundle/mattresses, brush removal, angler/hunter paths

properties.PROJECTPURPOSE: Beginning in August 2016, the DNR trout habitat crew began a trout habitat project on the lower portion of Wolf Creek in Governor Knowles State Forest.  Wolf Creek is a class II trout stream and is typically one of the better brown trout streams in Polk County.  The project encompass a 0.3 mile stretch of Wolf Creek near the snowmobile bridge.  The objective of this project was to increase in-stream habitat for brown trout and ultimately increase their abundance.  Through this project the stream was made more structurally complex by narrowing and deepening some areas, removing channel braiding, creating pools, and adding in-stream structural habitat in the form of large rocks, bank covers, wing deflectors, and wood.  Rock and wood were used to stabilize the toe of the stream bank (where needed) and used as backfill behind structures to prevent future erosion or structure failure from occurring.  Any exposed soils on the banks were seeded immediately following habitat improvement activities.  Angler access was also improved through stream bank brushing.

This project seeks funding for continuation of bank stabilization efforts on the Scuppernong Springs headwaters.  Biologs, brush bundles, boulders, root wads and course woody structure will be added to the stream to enhance habitat. Each year thousands of anglers fish this small trout stream located in the heart of the Kettle Moraine State Forest – Southern Unit.  Scuppernong Springs (WBIC 817600  Lat/Lon:42° 56' 8" N, 88° 28' 3" W), trout stream has excellent angler access with paved parking and breathtaking views of one of the largest continuous prairie restoration projects in the state.  The headwater area has been the focus of much restoration efforts including dam removal, bank stabilization and habitat enhancements.  This project will continue to improve and enhance this high quality stream and provide habitat for brook trout natural reproduction. External cooperation with three chapters of Trout Unlimited will create positive outreach. Before and after habitat improvement IBI scores will be calculated a fisheries report will be generated.  This project will also incorporate inter-disciplinary ecosystem management by working closely with water resource managers, endangered resources and the state forest naturalist.

The goal of the project was to go in and remove tag alder from the streams banks increasing angler accessibility as well as stabilizing the streams banks by allowing grasses to grow. In the future a more intensive project will be planned for the site.
properties.TECHNIQUESSTRUCTURES: brush removal
